svg.title: EVPN against VPLS on five dimensions, and the five route types that do the work
svg.desc: Left panel compares EVPN with VPLS on five rows: how MAC addresses are learned, the pseudowire or tunnel model, multihoming, broadcast handling and design effort. EVPN learns MACs from BGP, uses an ingress replication or multicast tunnel list rather than a full mesh of pseudowires, supports active-active multihoming, and confines broadcast to registered endpoints; the cost is more design work and a control plane that must be operated. Right panel lists the five EVPN route types: type 1 ethernet auto-discovery per segment, type 2 MAC and IP advertisement which is the workhorse, type 3 inclusive multicast for broadcast and unknown unicast, type 4 ethernet segment for multihoming, and type 5 IP prefix for layer-3 integration. A note explains that type 2 and type 5 are the two an enterprise engineer will actually read, and that type 3 is what replaces flooding.
svg.text: EVPN is VPLS with the learning moved from the data plane to BGP
Every improvement follows from that one change; the five route types are its vocabulary
FIVE DIMENSIONS
MAC learning: VPLS floods and learns from data → EVPN advertises MACs in BGP
Transport: VPLS full mesh of pseudowires → EVPN ingress replication or multicast
Multihoming: VPLS blocks one link → EVPN active-active with per-flow hashing
Broadcast: VPLS to every site → EVPN to the registered endpoints only
Effort: VPLS easy to start → EVPN needs a control plane you must operate
COST SIDE, STATED PLAINLY
One more BGP address family, one more set of route types, and a
team that must understand type 2 and type 5 output to troubleshoot.
An EVPN fault looks like “the MAC is not in BGP”, not like a cable.
THE FIVE ROUTE TYPES
Type 1 · ethernet auto-discovery: which segment is where, per ESI
Type 2 · MAC / IP advertisement: the workhorse. Carries the
MAC, the VNI, the next hop and the label or VNI to use.
Type 3 · inclusive multicast: the tunnel list for broadcast and
unknown unicast. This is what replaces flooding.
Type 4 · ethernet segment: which VTEPs serve a multihomed site
Type 5 · IP prefix route: layer-3 integration, prefix plus VNI
An enterprise engineer reads type 2 for layer-2 reachability and
type 5 for layer-3 reachability. Type 3 is the one that explains why
broadcast no longer reaches that site that was removed last week.
The judgement: EVPN does not make layer 2 better; it makes layer 2 visible. That is worth a control plane in a fabric with hundreds of switches and
worth very little in a five-site VPLS that has worked for years. Decide on the number of sites and the need for active-active, not on the acronym.
Migration note: an EVPN and a VPLS domain can coexist during a transition, but a bridge between them re-introduces the flooding you were removing. Plan the cut, not the interworking.
